name: Johann Gottlieb Fichte
biography: Cited, with Hegel, as an example of a German philosophical outlook 'totally unconnected with commerce,' and as subjective in temperament and doctrine. Introduced as Kant's immediate successor, who abandoned the 'thing-in-itself' and carried subjectivism to what Russell calls 'almost a kind of insanity,' becoming the theoretical founder of German nationalism via his Addresses to the German Nation. Mentioned as a lecturer Schopenhauer heard at Berlin and 'despised'; contrasted with Schopenhauer as one of the philosophers who discarded the thing-in-itself and thereby made knowledge, rather than will, metaphysically fundamental. Named as the philosopher with whom the 'intoxication of power' first invaded philosophy, a danger Russell fears modern instrumentalism risks reviving.
